 Spooky spending: Hong Kong bars predict 20% Halloween sales boost
 30 October 2026 
 By Amelie Maurice-Jones 
 Hong Kong’s bar industry is forecasting a 20% surge in business revenue during this year’s Halloween celebrations, which have been transformed into a month-long citywide campaign to boost hopes  of a tourism-led spending recovery. 
 Spooky festivities have been extended to span three consecutive weekends under the government’s ‘Hong Kong Halloween Month’, an initiative by the Tourism Board aimed at attracting more tourists and strengthening the city’s appeal as a nightlife hotspot. 
 So far, have the October weekends have seen tens of thousands of revellers descend on Hong Kong’s entertainment districts, with costumes ranging from zombies and Taoist priests to evil bartenders and impersonators of US President Donald Trump. 
 Joe Chan Hing, a representative of the Hong Kong Bar & Club Association, told The Standard (HK) that bars, restaurants and shopping malls had stepped up promotional efforts, including hiring DJs for live performances and launching social media campaigns. 
 The association has received encouraging feedback and reservation figures, Chan said, adding that festive decorations and free transport arrangements provided by the government were also expected to attract visitors. 
 “Backed by the strong festive atmosphere, along with the government’s various decorative installations and free transport arrangements, I am confident we will see a 20% increase in business over last year,” he said. 
 Hong Kong seeks to capitalise on mainland restrictions 
 The extended festivities come as Halloween celebrations in mainland China have faced tighter restrictions since 2023, when authorities in Shanghai detained some revellers over costumes that satirised social and economic issues. 
 Hong Kong businesses and tourism officials hope the city can capitalise on its more permissive festive atmosphere to attract visitors from across the border and international markets, boosting spending at bars, restaurants and retailers. 
 Allan Zeman, chairman of the Lan Kwai Fong Group, said Halloween had become an increasingly established part of Hong Kong’s nightlife after he helped introduce celebrations to the district more than 40 years ago. 
 He too estimated that the festivities generated an annual increase of 20-25% in food and beverage sales. 
 “Halloween, which was a Western holiday, was able to suddenly be accepted by the East now,” Zeman told Reuters .

 “So that’s really what Hong Kong is all about, ‘One country, two systems’. And so we can celebrate all together.” 
 Organisers said about 80,000 people celebrated in Lan Kwai Fong on 31 October 2025.  
 “Every year it gets stronger and people spend, and every year the costumes get more and more outrageous,” Zeman said, adding that the celebrations brought additional income to the district and supported its economic activity. 
 Carnival atmosphere draws crowds 
 Last weekend celebrations were certainly in full swing, with narrow streets filled with colourful costumes as onlookers took photographs and revellers gathered late into the night. Western horror characters appeared alongside figures from Chinese folklore, while some participants drew inspiration from the Covid pandemic – brandishing  swab kits while dressed in white protective suits. 
 A giant eyeball installation in Central’s Statue Square Gardens has also emerged as a popular attraction, while Halloween-themed displays have appeared in other parts of the city. 
 Huang Wei, a 34-year-old visitor from the southern Chinese technology hub of Shenzhen, told Reuters that the celebrations offered an opportunity to unwind. 
 “Being here gives me this real carnival vibe – it’s a great way to completely let loose and release ourselves after work,” he said, dressed as the Monkey King, a celebrated figure in Chinese mythology. 
 “I feel like the main reason for coming here is to free ourselves,” Huang added. He had travelled by metro with nine friends. 
 Tourism industry sees interest grow 
 The tourism industry is also anticipating a rise in independent travellers, while group tour bookings are expected to increase by a more modest 5-10%, Fanny Yeung Shuk-fan, executive director of the Travel Industry Council of Hong Kong, told The Standard HK . 
 She said that enquiries about Halloween travel recommendations had risen sharply, coming from both mainland Chinese visitors and overseas markets, including Malaysia, India and the Netherlands. 
 The council has provided tailored itinerary recommendations, with some travellers subsequently booking hotels and restaurants through its services. Yeung said enquiries from independent travellers had doubled compared with previous years.
